meva dṛṣṭimanujjhan samyagvyutpādakaḥ śāstrakāraḥ iti ucyate | saugataprabhṛtayastu tatkāriṇaśca taddveṣiṇa iti | etacca mayā kathāmukhatilake vitatya nirūpitam, anveṣyaṃ tat eva | apūrvāṃ praṇāmabhaṅgīṃ paśyan kaścit vyāmuhyedityā- (page 21) śayena ṭīkākārastatsamarthānāṃ karoti jayanamaskārādi iti | ādipadena vandanapradhyānaprabhṛti gṛhyate | iha dvayaniṣṭaṃ yat rūpaṃ, tat anyataramukhena pratipādyamānamubhayaviśrāntau paryavasāyayitayam | ghaṭo bhāsate, ghaṭaḥ paśyatīti hi ghaṭaṃ nirbhāsamānaṃ nirbhāsayatīti arthapratipattiḥ | ubhayaniṣṭhaṃ ca prahvatvamatra asyeti | utkarṣaśca ato'syeti | tat jayati-jayasi-jayetiśabdaprayoge parameśvarotkarṣamukhena pravṛtte'pi svātmanyagbhāvanātmakaṃ prahvatvamālambanīyamaparathā utkarṣasya anirvāhāt | evaṃ namo-namāmi-vande-ityādiprayoge svātmanyagbhāvanaparāmarśamukhena pravṛtte'pi īśvarotkarṣaviśrāntirāśra- yaṇīyā | tadidamubhayamekameva vastu dvyaṃśamapi sadiha śloke ā samantāt veditaṃ śabdena saṃmukhīkartavyasamastaśrotṛjanasphuṭaparāmarśayogyaṃ kṛtam | arthākṣiptaṃ hi sarvasya na gocaraḥ | atyantadurlabhaṃ dāsyam iti kathañcit ityanena uktamiti sutarāmātmaviṣaye nyagbhāvanamuktamuktam | mahāphalaṃ taddāsyam iti īśvarasya utkarṣaḥ dāsatvādeva svāmini īśvare labdhe punarīśvarapadaṃ māheśvaryaparyavasitameva | mahāphalapadena ṭīkākāraḥ samastasampatsamavāptihetum iti padaṃ pratyabhijñāviśeṣaṇamapi dāsyaviśeṣaṇamiti darśayati | vṛttau ca sūcito'yamartho dāsyalakṣmīḥ ityanena | dāsyaprabhavā lakṣmyaḥ samastāḥ saṃpadaḥ parameśvaraprasādāt labdhā yeneti | anyathā lakṣmīśabdopādānamasaṃgataṃ syāt bahvarthaviṣayatāprakaṭīkaraṇaṃ ca | vācāpi vā iti apiśabdāt kāyenāpīti mantavyam | tahāhi prahvatā ca utkarṣaṇaṃ ca tathā prakāśaparāmarśanarūpaṃ mānase saṃvedane tatsārarūpe ca vāktattve viśrāntam, natu jaḍe śarīre | tena manovāgātmakaṃ yadavibhaktaṃ saṃvicchakteḥ, tadeva arpayatā bhaktena (page 22) viśvamarpitaṃ bhagavati bhavatīti | tadāgame ------svātmānaṃ ca nivedayet | iti kathitam | nivedayediti ar
**The homage that is two-resting, and who is worthy to make it** The work opens with a prostration — and Abhinavagupta takes care to say what that prostration is. It is not a bending of the body, nor an empty sound. It is a *two-resting* homage: it rests at once in the Lord, whom it exalts, and in the devotee, whom it subordinates. The words of homage — "jaya," "victory," "namaḥ," "I bow," "I worship" — all move by one of these two directions, but each must culminate in the other. The "victory" of the Lord, to be real, requires the devotee's self-subordination; the "I bow" of the devotee, to be real, must rest in the Lord's excess. The two — the exalting and the subordinating — are one act, two aspects, made manifest by the single word of homage before the whole assembly. And the attaining of the Lord, the commentary tells us, is the attainment of *dāsya* — of servant-ness. And the servant-ness is extremely hard to get: that is what "kathaṃcit," "in some way," means. It is not a title; it is the very heart of the eligibility. And it is fruitful of the greatest good — for in becoming the servant of the Lord one attains the Lord's own excess, and all the fortunes (dāsyalakṣmī) follow from that servant-ness, granted by the Lord's grace. It is this that makes the devotee one who has attained all. The homage, moreover, is made in the mind and the speech — the mind-awareness and the word-essence — never in the inert body. "Even by speech," the text says, and by the "even" we understand "and by the body." But the prostration proper is the offering of the undivided mind-and-speech, which is the consciousness-power itself; and in offering that, the devotee offers the whole world to the Lord. As the teaching says: "he should offer his own self." The physical prostration — the bowing, the eight-limbed salutation — is only the upacāra, the visible mark by which the inner offering is inferred, not the primary act. And so the question of who is worthy. The objection arises: "the eligibility suits the explainer, who has attained; but how does it suit the mere listeners?" Abhinavagupta's answer is that the listener and the explainer are not two separate undertakings: the recognition is one, and the servant-ness is one. It is by this that the Lord's favor is won — the recognition is preceded by, and inferred from, the Lord's favor. And this is where the Gītā's four kinds of devotees come in — the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the knower. All of them, in their several gradations, are worthy of the servant-ness and of the recognition. The door is not narrow in the way of the world's ranks; it is narrow only in the way of the heart — for what is required is the self-subordination, the dāsya, and that, once attained, draws the Lord near. ---

> The commentary on "having attained, in some way" (kathaṃcit) opens up what the prostration is and who > is eligible to make it. The prostration is *two-resting*: it must, being conveyed through one of the > two [the Lord and the devotee], culminate in the rest of both. The "jaya" words, moved by the Lord's > excess, must have the self-subordinating as their support; the "namaḥ" words, moved by the > self-subordinating re-recollection, must rest in the Lord's excess. The two are one thing, two-aspect. > > The attainment of the Lord is the attainment of servant-ness (dāsya), and the servant-ness is the > heart of the eligibility. The four Gītā-devotees — the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the > seeker of wealth, the knower — are all eligible, in their gradations, for the dāsya and the > recognition. The "kathaṃcit" (in some way) says the dāsya is extremely hard to get; the more is the > self-subordination stated.
